notes.front: What is the Right to Financial Privacy Act (RFPA)?
notes.back: The 1978 federal law limiting when a government authority may obtain a customer's financial records from a financial institution.
notes.explanation: Access is barred unless the records are reasonably described and one of the routes the Act lists is used, such as the customer's authorisation or a warrant.
notes.example: Like a receptionist who will not hand over your file to an official who turns up without the right paperwork.
notes.source: 12 U.S.C. chapter 35 (Right to Financial Privacy Act), §3402
notes.evidence: no Government authority may have access to or obtain copies of, or the information contained in the financial records of any customer from a financial institution unless the financial records are reasonably described

notes.front: What is the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA)?
notes.back: The popular name for the federal record-keeping and reporting laws that require financial institutions to keep records and file reports useful in investigations.
notes.explanation: The name covers several provisions in titles 12 and 31, including the monetary transactions reporting subchapter that begins at 31 U.S.C. 5311.
notes.example: Like a duty to keep receipts and flag odd ones, imposed on banks so investigators can follow money later.
notes.source: 31 U.S.C. 5311 (Bank Secrecy Act, declaration of purpose), notes
notes.evidence: are each popularly known as the "Bank Secrecy Act".

notes.front: What is a suspicious activity report (SAR)?
notes.back: A report a financial institution files on a suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation.
notes.explanation: The Treasury Secretary may require such reports from institutions and their directors, officers, employees and agents.
notes.example: Like a shop assistant quietly telling the manager about a customer paying in odd ways, but filed with a government agency.
notes.source: 31 U.S.C. 5318 (compliance and suspicious transaction reporting), §5318(g)(1)
notes.evidence: to report any suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation

notes.front: What is the Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA)?
notes.back: The 1986 Act that extended federal wiretap law to electronic communications and added rules on stored communications and pen registers.
notes.explanation: Its short-title note covers amendments to the wiretap chapter and the enactment of sections 2701 and 3121, which begin the stored communications and pen register chapters.
notes.example: Like updating a law about opening letters so it also covers email.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 119 (Wiretap Act, ECPA title I), short title note
notes.evidence: may be cited as the 'Electronic Communications Privacy Act of 1986'.

notes.front: What does the Wiretap Act, ECPA title I, prohibit?
notes.back: Intentionally intercepting, or procuring another to intercept, any wire, oral or electronic communication, unless the chapter provides otherwise.
notes.explanation: Its protection reaches communications in transit; stored communications are dealt with in the next chapter.
notes.example: Like a ban on steaming open letters while they are in the post.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 119 (Wiretap Act, ECPA title I), §2511(1)(a)
notes.evidence: intentionally intercepts, endeavors to intercept, or procures any other person to intercept or endeavor to intercept, any wire, oral, or electronic communication

notes.front: What is the Stored Communications Act (SCA)?
notes.back: ECPA title II (18 U.S.C. chapter 121), which protects communications held in electronic storage and governs access to them and to customer records.
notes.explanation: Its first offence is intentionally accessing a communications facility without authorisation and obtaining, altering or blocking a stored communication.
notes.example: Like the Wiretap Act, but for letters already delivered and sitting in the mailbox.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 121 (Stored Communications Act, ECPA title II), §2701(a)
notes.evidence: intentionally accesses without authorization a facility through which an electronic communication service is provided

notes.front: What is a pen register?
notes.back: A device or process recording dialling, routing, addressing or signalling information from a communication, but not its contents.
notes.explanation: A trap and trace device is its counterpart for incoming information identifying the source.
notes.example: Like logging the addresses on envelopes without opening them.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 206 (pen registers and trap and trace devices), §3127(3)
notes.evidence: a device or process which records or decodes dialing, routing, addressing, or signaling information transmitted by an instrument or facility from which a wire or electronic communication is transmitted, provided, however, that such information shall not include the contents of any communication

notes.front: What is the Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act (CALEA)?
notes.back: The 1994 federal law requiring telecommunications carriers to build in the capability to support lawful interception.
notes.explanation: It was title I of Pub. L. 103–414 and is codified at 47 U.S.C. chapter 9, subchapter I.
notes.example: Like building a door into a wall so authorised inspectors can get in without knocking it down.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. chapter 9, subchapter I (CALEA), short title note
notes.evidence: may be cited as the 'Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act'.
introduces: Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act
uses: Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act

notes.front: What is the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA)?
notes.back: The 1978 federal law setting procedures, including court orders, for electronic surveillance and other collection for foreign intelligence purposes.
notes.explanation: It is codified at 50 U.S.C. chapter 36, which also covers physical searches, pen registers, business records and targeting of people abroad.
notes.example: Like a criminal warrant system, but for spying on foreign powers and their agents.
notes.source: 50 U.S.C. chapter 36 (Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act), short title note
notes.evidence: may be cited as the 'Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978'.

notes.front: What is the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC)?
notes.back: 11 district court judges, from at least seven judicial circuits, designated by the Chief Justice to hear applications for FISA surveillance orders.
notes.explanation: At least 3 of them must live within 20 miles of the District of Columbia.
notes.example: Like a magistrate who signs search warrants, but a special panel for intelligence surveillance.
notes.source: 50 U.S.C. chapter 36 (Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act), §1803(a)(1)
notes.evidence: The Chief Justice of the United States shall publicly designate 11 district court judges from at least seven of the United States judicial circuits

notes.front: What is Section 702 of FISA?
notes.back: The provision, added in 2008, letting the Attorney General and Director of National Intelligence authorise targeting non-U.S. persons reasonably believed to be abroad.
notes.explanation: It is FISA title VII, section 702, codified at 50 U.S.C. 1881a and added by Pub. L. 110–261, the FISA Amendments Act of 2008.
notes.example: Like a standing licence to collect from overseas targets, reviewed by the court rather than approved case by case.
notes.source: 50 U.S.C. chapter 36 (Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act), §1881a source credit
notes.evidence: Pub. L. 95–511, title VII, §702, as added Pub. L. 110–261, title I, §101(a)(2), July 10, 2008

notes.front: What is a national security letter (NSL)?
notes.back: A written request from the Federal Bureau of Investigation compelling a communications provider to hand over subscriber and toll billing records.
notes.explanation: Section 2709 obliges the provider to comply with a request made under subsection (b).
notes.example: Like an administrative subpoena, but issued by the Federal Bureau of Investigation for counter-intelligence.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 121 (Stored Communications Act, ECPA title II), §2709(a)
notes.evidence: A wire or electronic communication service provider shall comply with a request for subscriber information and toll billing records information, or electronic communication transactional records in its custody or possession made by the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation

notes.front: What is the USA PATRIOT Act?
notes.back: The 2001 counter-terrorism Act (Pub. L. 107–56) that, among much else, rewrote FISA's business records provision in its section 215.
notes.explanation: The business records section of FISA carries the source credit Pub. L. 107–56, title II, §215; the Act's short title is recorded in the notes to 18 U.S.C. 1.
notes.example: Like a toolkit Congress handed investigators after 11 September 2001.
notes.source: 50 U.S.C. chapter 36 (Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act), §1862 source credit
notes.evidence: as added Pub. L. 107–56, title II, §215, Oct. 26, 2001

notes.front: What is the USA FREEDOM Act?
notes.back: The 2015 Act (Pub. L. 114–23) that amended FISA and national security letters, including by requiring requests to rest on a specific selection term.
notes.explanation: For national security letters it inserted the requirement to use a term that specifically identifies a person, entity, telephone number or account.
notes.example: Like replacing a trawl net with a fishing line: requests must name what they are after.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 121 (Stored Communications Act, ECPA title II), §2709 amendment notes, 2015
notes.evidence: Pub. L. 114–23, §501(a), substituted "may, using a term that specifically identifies a person, entity, telephone number, or account as the basis for a request" for "may"

notes.front: What is the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act (CISA)?
notes.back: The 2015 federal law authorising private entities to monitor their systems and share cyber threat indicators, with liability protection.
notes.explanation: It forms 6 U.S.C. chapter 6, subchapter I, within the Cybersecurity Act of 2015.
notes.example: Like a neighbourhood watch that lets firms swap descriptions of burglars without being sued for it.
notes.source: 6 U.S.C. chapter 6, subchapter I (Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015), notes
notes.evidence: the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 which comprises this subchapter

notes.front: What is the Privacy Protection Act of 1980 (PPA)?
notes.back: The federal law making it generally unlawful for government officers investigating crime to search for or seize journalists' and publishers' work product.
notes.explanation: It protects materials held by a person reasonably believed to intend public communication, such as a newspaper, book or broadcast.
notes.example: Like a shield around a newsroom's notebooks against police searches.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. chapter 21A, subchapter I (Privacy Protection Act of 1980), §2000aa(a)
notes.evidence: it shall be unlawful for a government officer or employee, in connection with the investigation or prosecution of a criminal offense, to search for or seize any work product materials

notes.front: Whose access to financial records does the RFPA restrict?
notes.back: A "Government authority": any agency or department of the United States, or its officers, employees or agents.
notes.explanation: The definition is federal, so state and local agencies fall outside it.
notes.source: 12 U.S.C. chapter 35 (Right to Financial Privacy Act), §3401(3)
notes.evidence: "Government authority" means any agency or department of the United States, or any officer, employee, or agent thereof

notes.front: What are two routes by which a federal authority may lawfully obtain customer records under the RFPA?
notes.back: Among others: the customer's authorisation, and a search warrant.
notes.explanation: The Act also lists an administrative subpoena or summons, a judicial subpoena and a formal written request, each meeting its own section.
notes.source: 12 U.S.C. chapter 35 (Right to Financial Privacy Act), §3402
notes.evidence: such financial records are disclosed in response to a search warrant which meets the requirements of section 3406 of this title

notes.front: For how long may a customer authorise disclosure of records under the RFPA?
notes.back: For a period not exceeding three months.
notes.explanation: The signed, dated statement must also say the customer may revoke it before disclosure and identify the records and purposes.
notes.source: 12 U.S.C. chapter 35 (Right to Financial Privacy Act), §3404(a)
notes.evidence: authorizes such disclosure for a period not in excess of three months

notes.front: Does the RFPA let an institution withhold information that a federal statute requires it to report?
notes.back: No. The Act does not authorise withholding information required to be reported under any federal statute or rule.
notes.explanation: This is how reports under the record-keeping and reporting laws sit alongside the RFPA.
notes.source: 12 U.S.C. chapter 35 (Right to Financial Privacy Act), §3413(d)
notes.evidence: information required to be reported in accordance with any Federal statute or rule promulgated thereunder

notes.front: According to 31 U.S.C. 5311, what are two purposes of the Bank Secrecy Act reporting rules?
notes.back: Among others: requiring reports highly useful in criminal, tax or regulatory investigations, and preventing money laundering and terrorist financing.
notes.explanation: Other listed purposes include tracking criminally sourced money and assessing laundering and fraud risks.
notes.source: 31 U.S.C. 5311 (Bank Secrecy Act, declaration of purpose), §5311
notes.evidence: require certain reports or records that are highly useful in- (A) criminal, tax, or regulatory investigations, risk assessments, or proceedings

notes.front: Once a suspicious transaction is reported, may the institution tell the customer involved?
notes.back: No. It may not notify anyone involved that the transaction was reported, or reveal information showing it.
notes.explanation: The bar extends to current and former directors, officers, employees and contractors of the institution.
notes.source: 31 U.S.C. 5318 (compliance and suspicious transaction reporting), §5318(g)(2)(A)
notes.evidence: may notify any person involved in the transaction that the transaction has been reported

notes.front: Under the Wiretap Act, what does "intercept" mean?
notes.back: The aural or other acquisition of the contents of a wire, electronic or oral communication through any electronic, mechanical or other device.
notes.explanation: The definition turns on acquiring contents, which separates it from recording routing information.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 119 (Wiretap Act, ECPA title I), §2510(4)
notes.evidence: "intercept" means the aural or other acquisition of the contents of any wire, electronic, or oral communication through the use of any electronic, mechanical, or other device

notes.front: When may a private person lawfully intercept a communication under the Wiretap Act consent exception?
notes.back: When that person is a party to it, or one party has given prior consent, unless the purpose is a criminal or tortious act.
notes.explanation: Federal law therefore needs only one party's consent; the purpose proviso removes the protection for crimes and torts.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 119 (Wiretap Act, ECPA title I), §2511(2)(d)
notes.evidence: where such person is a party to the communication or where one of the parties to the communication has given prior consent to such interception unless such communication is intercepted for the purpose of committing any criminal or tortious act

notes.front: Besides probable cause, what must a judge find before approving a federal wiretap order?
notes.back: That normal investigative procedures have failed, seem unlikely to succeed, or would be too dangerous.
notes.explanation: The judge must also find probable cause about the offence and that the interception will capture communications about it.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 119 (Wiretap Act, ECPA title I), §2518(3)(c)
notes.evidence: normal investigative procedures have been tried and have failed or reasonably appear to be unlikely to succeed if tried or to be too dangerous

notes.front: What may a public electronic communication service not do with the contents of stored communications, under the SCA?
notes.back: Knowingly divulge them to any person or entity, unless an exception applies.
notes.explanation: The exceptions include the lawful consent of the originator, an addressee or the intended recipient.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 121 (Stored Communications Act, ECPA title II), §2702(a)(1)
notes.evidence: a person or entity providing an electronic communication service to the public shall not knowingly divulge to any person or entity the contents of a communication while in electronic storage by that service

notes.front: What must a government entity obtain to compel a provider to disclose communications in electronic storage for 180 days or less?
notes.back: A warrant issued using the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, or equivalent state warrant procedures.
notes.explanation: The warrant requirement applies to the contents of wire or electronic communications held by a communication service provider.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 121 (Stored Communications Act, ECPA title II), §2703(a)
notes.evidence: that is in electronic storage in an electronic communications system for one hundred and eighty days or less, only pursuant to a warrant

notes.front: What are two subscriber details a provider must disclose to a government entity using an administrative subpoena under the SCA?
notes.back: Among others: name and address.
notes.explanation: Session records, length and type of service, subscriber numbers and payment sources are also listed.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 121 (Stored Communications Act, ECPA title II), §2703(c)(2)
notes.evidence: shall disclose to a governmental entity the— (A) name; (B) address

notes.front: On what certification does a court issue a federal pen register order?
notes.back: The government attorney's certification that the information likely to be obtained is relevant to an ongoing criminal investigation.
notes.explanation: The court enters the order ex parte once it finds that certification has been made.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 206 (pen registers and trap and trace devices), §3123(a)(1)
notes.evidence: the attorney for the Government has certified to the court that the information likely to be obtained by such installation and use is relevant to an ongoing criminal investigation

notes.front: What capability does CALEA require of a telecommunications carrier?
notes.back: To isolate and enable the government, under a court order or other lawful authorisation, to intercept its subscribers' wire and electronic communications.
notes.explanation: Carriers must also enable access to call-identifying information that is reasonably available to them.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. chapter 9, subchapter I (CALEA), §1002(a)(1)
notes.evidence: expeditiously isolating and enabling the government, pursuant to a court order or other lawful authorization, to intercept, to the exclusion of any other communications, all wire and electronic communications carried by the carrier
uses: Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act

notes.front: What probable cause must a FISA electronic surveillance order rest on?
notes.back: That the target is a foreign power or an agent of a foreign power.
notes.explanation: No U.S. person may be treated as such an agent solely for activities protected by the First Amendment.
notes.source: 50 U.S.C. chapter 36 (Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act), §1805(a)(2)
notes.evidence: the target of the electronic surveillance is a foreign power or an agent of a foreign power

notes.front: For how long may a Section 702 authorisation run?
notes.back: Up to 1 year from its effective date.
notes.explanation: The Attorney General and Director of National Intelligence authorise it jointly, after a court order or an emergency determination.
notes.source: 50 U.S.C. chapter 36 (Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act), §1881a(a)
notes.evidence: may authorize jointly, for a period of up to 1 year from the effective date of the authorization, the targeting of persons reasonably believed to be located outside the United States

notes.front: May Section 702 be used to target a U.S. person who is abroad?
notes.back: No. It may not intentionally target a United States person reasonably believed to be outside the United States.
notes.explanation: The same limits bar targeting anyone known to be in the United States.
notes.source: 50 U.S.C. chapter 36 (Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act), §1881a(b)(3)
notes.evidence: may not intentionally target a United States person reasonably believed to be located outside the United States

notes.front: What does the sunset note to Section 702, as amended by Pub. L. 119–87 (30 April 2026), provide?
notes.back: That the section is repealed effective 12 June 2026, except as provided in the transition section of the 2008 Act.
notes.explanation: Congress has moved this date many times, so check the current code before relying on it.
notes.source: 50 U.S.C. chapter 36 (Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act), §1881a, Repeal of Section note
notes.evidence: Pub. L. 119–87, §1(a)(1), Apr. 30, 2026, 140 Stat. 811, provided that, except as provided in section 404 of Pub. L. 110–261, set out as a note under section 1801 of this title, effective June 12, 2026, this section is repealed.

notes.front: What must the Federal Bureau of Investigation certify to obtain toll billing records by national security letter?
notes.back: That the records are relevant to an authorised investigation to protect against international terrorism or clandestine intelligence activities.
notes.explanation: The certification is made in writing to the provider by the Director or a senior designee.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 121 (Stored Communications Act, ECPA title II), §2709(b)(1)
notes.evidence: relevant to an authorized investigation to protect against international terrorism or clandestine intelligence activities

notes.front: What may a provider receiving a national security letter be barred from telling anyone?
notes.back: That the Federal Bureau of Investigation has sought or obtained access to information or records under the letter.
notes.explanation: The bar applies where a certification is issued and notice of the right to judicial review is given.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 121 (Stored Communications Act, ECPA title II), §2709(c)(1)(A)
notes.evidence: shall disclose to any person that the Federal Bureau of Investigation has sought or obtained access to information or records under this section

notes.front: Since 15 March 2020, how does FISA's business records section 1862 read?
notes.back: As it read on 25 October 2001: orders for records of common carriers, public accommodation, storage or vehicle rental facilities.
notes.explanation: Pub. L. 109–177 of 2006, as repeatedly amended, made the section revert on that date to its wording of 25 October 2001.
notes.source: 50 U.S.C. chapter 36 (Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act), §1862 amendment notes
notes.evidence: amended section effective Mar. 15, 2020, so as to read as it read on Oct. 25, 2001

notes.front: Which systems does CISA let a private entity monitor for cybersecurity purposes?
notes.back: Its own information systems, and another entity's systems with that entity's authorisation and written consent.
notes.explanation: The authority also reaches information stored on, processed by or transiting the monitored systems.
notes.source: 6 U.S.C. chapter 6, subchapter I (Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015), §1503(a)(1)
notes.evidence: a private entity may, for cybersecurity purposes, monitor— (A) an information system of such private entity; (B) an information system of another non-Federal entity, upon the authorization and written consent of such other entity

notes.front: What must a non-federal entity do before sharing a cyber threat indicator under CISA?
notes.back: Review it and remove personal information of a specific individual not directly related to a cybersecurity threat, or use a technical capability that does so.
notes.explanation: The duty covers information the entity knows, at the time of sharing, to be personal or identifying.
notes.source: 6 U.S.C. chapter 6, subchapter I (Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015), §1503(d)(2)
notes.evidence: contains any information not directly related to a cybersecurity threat that the non-Federal entity knows at the time of sharing to be personal information of a specific individual

notes.front: Until when does the current text of CISA give its authorities effect?
notes.back: Until 11 December 2026, after two 2026 extensions.
notes.explanation: Actions taken before the provisions lapse remain covered, so check the code for any further extension.
notes.source: 6 U.S.C. chapter 6, subchapter I (Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015), §1510(a)
notes.evidence: during the period beginning on December 18, 2015 and ending on December 11, 2026

notes.front: What are two situations in which officers may still search for a journalist's work product under the PPA?
notes.back: Probable cause that the holder committed the related offence, and immediate seizure needed to prevent death or serious bodily injury.
notes.explanation: The first exception does not apply where the offence is merely receiving, possessing or withholding the materials, subject to listed exceptions.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. chapter 21A, subchapter I (Privacy Protection Act of 1980), §2000aa(a)(2)
notes.evidence: there is reason to believe that the immediate seizure of such materials is necessary to prevent the death of, or serious bodily injury to, a human being

notes.front: A city police department asks a bank for a customer's statements. Does the federal RFPA govern the request?
notes.back: B: no, its "Government authority" means federal agencies and departments.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, it covers all government bodies
B) No, its "Government authority" means federal agencies and departments
C) Yes, but only if the customer is a corporation
D) No, the RFPA was repealed by the Bank Secrecy Act
notes.choicesExplained: A: the definition names agencies of the United States only. C: corporations are not "persons" under the Act. D: both laws remain in the code and work together.
notes.explanation: The RFPA defines a Government authority as a U.S. agency or department, or its officers, employees or agents.
notes.source: 12 U.S.C. chapter 35 (Right to Financial Privacy Act), §3401(3)
notes.evidence: "Government authority" means any agency or department of the United States

notes.front: A bank has filed a report about a customer's unusual cash deposits. The customer calls and asks whether the bank has reported him. What should staff do?
notes.back: C: not reveal that a report was filed.
notes.choices:
A) Confirm it, as customers have a right to know
B) Confirm it only if the customer asks in writing
C) Not reveal that a report was filed
D) Close the account and explain why
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: the statute bars notifying anyone involved that the transaction was reported. D: explaining why would reveal the report.
notes.explanation: Section 5318(g)(2) forbids telling anyone involved in the transaction that it has been reported.
notes.source: 31 U.S.C. 5318 (compliance and suspicious transaction reporting), §5318(g)(2)(A)
notes.evidence: or otherwise reveal any information that would reveal that the transaction has been reported

notes.front: A customer secretly records her own phone call with a company's sales agent to keep a record of promises made. Under the federal Wiretap Act, is this lawful?
notes.back: D: yes, she is a party to the call and has no criminal or tortious purpose.
notes.choices:
A) No, every party must consent
B) No, only law enforcement may record calls
C) Yes, but only if she announces it
D) Yes, she is a party to the call and has no criminal or tortious purpose
notes.choicesExplained: A: federal law needs only one party's consent. B: the private-party exception covers her. C: being a party is enough; no announcement is required by this exception.
notes.explanation: A party to a communication may intercept it unless the purpose is to commit a criminal or tortious act.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 119 (Wiretap Act, ECPA title I), §2511(2)(d)
notes.evidence: where such person is a party to the communication

notes.front: Investigators want a webmail provider to hand over the contents of an email stored for 60 days. What does the SCA require them to get?
notes.back: A: a warrant.
notes.choices:
A) A warrant
B) An administrative subpoena
C) A letter from the prosecutor
D) Nothing, if the provider agrees
notes.choicesExplained: B: a subpoena reaches basic subscriber records, not stored contents of this age. C: no such route exists. D: the provider may not knowingly divulge contents without an exception.
notes.explanation: Compelled disclosure of contents in storage for 180 days or less needs a warrant.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 121 (Stored Communications Act, ECPA title II), §2703(a)
notes.evidence: for one hundred and eighty days or less, only pursuant to a warrant

notes.front: Police want to log the numbers dialled from a suspect's phone, but not hear any calls. Which tool is this?
notes.back: B: a pen register.
notes.choices:
A) A Wiretap Act interception
B) A pen register
C) A FISA surveillance order
D) A CALEA capability
notes.choicesExplained: A: interception means acquiring contents. C: FISA is for foreign intelligence targets. D: CALEA sets carrier capability; it is not an investigative order.
notes.explanation: A pen register records dialling and routing information but not the contents of a communication.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 206 (pen registers and trap and trace devices), §3127(3)
notes.evidence: such information shall not include the contents of any communication

notes.front: An analyst proposes using Section 702 to target a U.S. citizen working in Singapore. Is that allowed?
notes.back: C: no, Section 702 may not intentionally target a U.S. person abroad.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because she is outside the United States
B) Yes, with the Attorney General's written approval
C) No, Section 702 may not intentionally target a U.S. person abroad
D) Yes, if the FISC is told afterwards
notes.choicesExplained: A: location abroad is not enough when the target is a U.S. person. B and D: no approval or notice overrides the statutory limit.
notes.explanation: Section 702 limits bar intentionally targeting a United States person reasonably believed to be outside the United States.
notes.source: 50 U.S.C. chapter 36 (Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act), §1881a(b)(3)
notes.evidence: may not intentionally target a United States person reasonably believed to be located outside the United States

notes.front: An application for electronic surveillance of a suspected agent of a foreign power is filed. Which body hears it?
notes.back: D: the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court.
notes.choices:
A) The local federal magistrate judge
B) The Federal Communications Commission
C) The state attorney general
D) The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court
notes.choicesExplained: A: FISA surveillance applications go to the specially designated judges. B: the FCC is a regulator, not a court. C: a state attorney general does not grant FISA orders.
notes.explanation: The designated judges form a court with jurisdiction to hear applications for FISA surveillance orders.
notes.source: 50 U.S.C. chapter 36 (Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act), §1803(a)(1)
notes.evidence: shall constitute a court which shall have jurisdiction to hear applications for and grant orders approving electronic surveillance anywhere within the United States

notes.front: A phone company receives a national security letter with a nondisclosure certification. A journalist asks whether it has received one. What may the company say?
notes.back: A: it may not disclose that the Bureau sought or obtained its records.
notes.choices:
A) It may not disclose that the Bureau sought or obtained its records
B) It may confirm receipt but not the contents
C) It may disclose freely, as letters are not court orders
D) It must refer the journalist to the FISC
notes.choicesExplained: B: even confirming receipt reveals that access was sought. C: the statute itself imposes the bar. D: no such referral is required.
notes.explanation: Where the certification is issued, the provider may not tell anyone the Bureau sought or obtained access.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 121 (Stored Communications Act, ECPA title II), §2709(c)(1)(A)
notes.evidence: shall disclose to any person that the Federal Bureau of Investigation has sought or obtained access to information or records under this section

notes.front: After the USA FREEDOM Act, which national security letter request fits section 2709?
notes.back: B: a request naming a specific telephone number as its basis.
notes.choices:
A) A request for all subscribers in one area code
B) A request naming a specific telephone number as its basis
C) A request for every customer's toll records
D) A request with no stated basis
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D: each lacks a term specifically identifying a person, entity, telephone number or account.
notes.explanation: Since 2015 the Bureau must use a term that specifically identifies a person, entity, telephone number or account as the basis for a request.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 121 (Stored Communications Act, ECPA title II), §2709(b)
notes.evidence: may, using a term that specifically identifies a person, entity, telephone number, or account as the basis for a request

notes.front: Which Act first added FISA's current business records section, 50 U.S.C. 1862, in the form cited in its source credit?
notes.back: C: the USA PATRIOT Act of 2001.
notes.choices:
A) The Electronic Communications Privacy Act of 1986
B) The Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act
C) The USA PATRIOT Act of 2001
D) The Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015
notes.choicesExplained: A: ECPA reformed wiretap and stored communications law. B: CALEA concerns carrier capability. D: CISA concerns sharing threat indicators.
notes.explanation: The source credit reads Pub. L. 95–511, title V, §502, as added by Pub. L. 107–56, section 215.
notes.source: 50 U.S.C. chapter 36 (Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act), §1862 source credit
notes.evidence: as added Pub. L. 107–56, title II, §215, Oct. 26, 2001
uses: Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act

notes.front: A retailer wants to share a phishing email with other firms as a threat indicator. It includes a customer's name unrelated to the attack. What does CISA require first?
notes.back: D: remove the personal information not directly related to the threat.
notes.choices:
A) Obtain the customer's written consent
B) Share only with the federal government
C) Nothing, as sharing is protected
D) Remove the personal information not directly related to the threat
notes.choicesExplained: A: CISA's duty is removal, not consent. B: sharing with other non-federal entities is allowed. C: protection depends on sharing in accordance with the Act.
notes.explanation: Before sharing, a non-federal entity must remove known personal information not directly related to a cybersecurity threat.
notes.source: 6 U.S.C. chapter 6, subchapter I (Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015), §1503(d)(2)
notes.evidence: personal information of a specific individual or information that identifies a specific individual and remove such information

notes.front: Police investigating a burglary want to search a newspaper's newsroom for a reporter's notes about it. Neither the reporter nor the paper is suspected. What does the PPA say?
notes.back: A: the search is unlawful unless an exception applies, such as preventing death or serious injury.
notes.choices:
A) The search is unlawful unless an exception applies, such as preventing death or serious injury
B) The search is lawful with any warrant
C) The search is lawful because the notes are evidence
D) The PPA covers only books, not newspapers
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the Act bars the search even where materials are evidence, subject to its exceptions. D: newspapers are expressly covered.
notes.explanation: The Act makes it unlawful to search for or seize work product held for public communication, subject to narrow exceptions.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. chapter 21A, subchapter I (Privacy Protection Act of 1980), §2000aa(a)
notes.evidence: possessed by a person reasonably believed to have a purpose to disseminate to the public a newspaper, book, broadcast, or other similar form of public communication

notes.front: A carrier launches a new voice service with no way to isolate one subscriber's calls for a court-ordered intercept. Which law does this design breach?
notes.back: C: the Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act.
notes.choices:
A) The Stored Communications Act
B) The Right to Financial Privacy Act
C) The Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act
D) The Privacy Protection Act of 1980
notes.choicesExplained: A: the SCA governs access to stored communications, not carrier design. B: the RFPA concerns financial records. D: the PPA protects journalists' materials.
notes.explanation: CALEA requires carriers to be able to isolate and enable lawful interception of subscribers' communications.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. chapter 9, subchapter I (CALEA), §1002(a)(1)
notes.evidence: expeditiously isolating and enabling the government, pursuant to a court order or other lawful authorization, to intercept
uses: Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act

notes.front: A bank files a required report on a large cash transaction with the Treasury without the customer's authorisation. Which statement is right?
notes.back: D: the RFPA does not authorise withholding information a federal statute requires to be reported.
notes.choices:
A) The bank breaches the RFPA, which needs customer authorisation
B) The bank needs a search warrant first
C) The report is lawful only for corporate customers
D) The RFPA does not authorise withholding information a federal statute requires to be reported
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: required federal reporting is carved out of the RFPA's limits. C: the carve-out does not depend on the customer type.
notes.explanation: Section 3413(d) says nothing in the RFPA authorises withholding information required to be reported under a federal statute or rule.
notes.source: 12 U.S.C. chapter 35 (Right to Financial Privacy Act), §3413(d)
notes.evidence: required to be reported in accordance with any Federal statute or rule promulgated thereunder
